I'm trying to identify the most severe steric clash by scanning residue pairs for atoms sitting unusually close together, checking cysteine sulfurs and other side chains for suspiciously tight distances.

With over a thousand atoms, checking everything by hand isn't practical, so I'm narrowing my search to side-chain tips that seem likely to overlap with backbone atoms in the same spatial region, since that's a common source of clashes.

I'm now checking the guanidinium groups of the arginine residues one by one against nearby atoms to see if any distances fall below a clash threshold. So far ARG29, ARG30, and ARG58 don't show obvious close contacts with the residues I've compared them to.

Continuing through ARG60, ARG68, ARG77, ARG100, and ARG106, I'm not finding any distances small enough to flag as steric clashes with the nearby atoms I'm checking.

Moving on to ARG111, ARG115, ARG130, and ARG135, I check each guanidinium group's NH1/NH2/NE positions against neighboring residue side chains, and again nothing comes close enough to count as a clash — the closest candidate near GLU110/ARG115 is still around 3.6 Å apart.

With ARG149 marking the end of the arginine set, I'm now shifting to scan the lysine residues, starting with LYS41's NZ position.

Checking LYS87's NZ against nearby GLY84 and THR85 atoms gives distances around 3.2 Å — still too far for a real clash. I consider searching for close contacts between acidic and basic side chains, but realize the clash might not be electrostatic at all, so I try scanning backbone atoms across distant sequence positions and even consider binning coordinates into 3 Å cells to narrow things down, though that's tough to do by hand. I decide to focus on the protein core and look at TRP53's ring atom positions to see if anything there stands out.

Testing distances between TRP53's ring, PHE47's ring, and various VAL131, ILE104, and LEU91 side chains, everything keeps coming back too far apart — nothing under 4 Å. I keep working through pairs like HIS92 and LEU94 side chains near ILE104, still without finding the clash I'm looking for.

Deciding to switch strategies, I want to scan CA-to-CA distances between non-sequential residues to spot suspiciously close backbone atoms, so I'm listing out CA coordinates for residues 19 through 29 to compare pairwise distances across the chain.

Still computing coordinate points...

I'm scanning through the remaining CA coordinates, then checking non-adjacent CA pairs for distances under 5 Å to spot potential clashes or unexpected contacts. One pair, residues 86 and 109, comes out to about 4.18 Å apart, which is tighter than typical for non-bonded residues, so I'm digging into their side-chain atom distances to see if this is a real steric issue.

Since checking every atom near the 86-109 pair doesn't turn up anything severe, I keep scanning other CA pairs across the structure for anything under 4.5 Å, but nothing else stands out. I realize CA-CA screening alone won't catch all side-chain clashes, so I decide to shift strategy and look specifically at atoms belonging to long side chains instead.

Now I'm checking exposed side chains like GLN23, GLU20, and GLU22 individually, measuring distances to nearby residues in similar coordinate regions, but each one seems isolated enough that there's no real steric conflict.

Since scanning atom-by-atom is too slow, I try dividing the structure into spatial grid cells, but that still feels impractical for finding one dominant clash. I switch tactics and start checking aromatic and histidine side chains for ring overlaps, comparing HIS54's ring atoms against nearby LYS66, SER52, and ARG135 positions to see if any distances look suspiciously short.

Moving through more histidines, I check HIS65's ring against GLN74, ALA70, ILE61, and ALA62, finding the closest contact around 3.8 Å which isn't alarming. I do the same for HIS92 against ILE104 and LEU91, and then HIS105, checking its ring nitrogens against CYS120's sulfur atom, finding a roughly 4.0 Å gap that's still within normal range.

I notice TYR32's hydroxyl sits about 2.83 Å from HIS105's ND1, which reads as a genuine hydrogen bond, and I confirm TYR32's CZ carbon is a bit farther out at 3.5 Å. Then I move to HIS137, comparing it against ARG135's guanidinium nitrogen and finding no problematic clash there.

Now I'm compiling the list of aromatic residues to check next—tyrosines, phenylalanines, and tryptophans—and starting to lay out the ring coordinates for TRP144 and TRP148 so I can compare their positions against each other.

I finish mapping TRP148's ring atoms and calculate the distance between TRP144's CZ2 and TRP148's NE1, landing around 3.4 Å, which seems acceptable. I check a few more atom pairs between these two tryptophans and PHE147, none of which raise concerns.

Since nothing here explains the clash, I consider that it might instead involve backbone-to-backbone contacts between distant sequence segments, so I start pulling coordinates for residues 135, 136, 122, and 134 to examine that region more closely, focusing on ARG135's and GLU136's side chains.

After checking distances involving GLU136, CYS120, TYR78, and nearby residues, nothing stands out as problematic either. I'm starting to think I need a more systematic approach, like building a spatial hash with 5 Å cells to only compare side-chain atoms from residues separated by more than two positions in sequence, since scanning pairs individually isn't converging on the clash.

Given 131 residues, a full CA-CA distance matrix is too large to check by hand, so I'm trying to bin CA coordinates into ~6 Å cells to identify spatially close residue clusters instead—working through the floor-division math for each residue's x, y, z cell indices to group them by region.

Since severe clashes usually involve tiny distances between two side chains, I'm going through the remaining unchecked residues—lysines, methionines, glutamates, aspartates, asparagines, serines, and cysteines—and computing their side chain atom coordinates one by one, starting with MET40's CB, CG, and SD positions, to look for any suspiciously overlapping atoms.

I check MET40's CE against nearby PHE35 ring atoms and other neighbors, finding nothing closer than about 3.6 Å, so that region looks fine. I then move through LYS41 and LYS66, both of which appear solvent-exposed with no obvious clashes, and start examining LYS95's side chain atoms against nearby GLU22 to see if the NZ-OE1 distance is problematic.

Checking further, NZ to OE1 comes out to 2.6 Å, which reads as a legitimate salt-bridge hydrogen bond rather than a clash, and the CE-OE1 distance of 3.1 is also acceptable. I continue through LYS114, checking its NZ against nearby ARG149 and GLU146 atoms and finding distances around 3.8-4.5 Å, which is fine, then move to LYS127 (exposed, no issues) and LYS87 (checking against GLY84 and THR108, both too far to matter). I'm now starting on GLU45's side chain geometry.

Continuing through the remaining aspartate residues, checking ASP48, ASP64, ASP97/98, ASP117, ASP133, and ASP140 coordinates against nearby basic residues to confirm they're all solvent-exposed without unexpected salt bridges.

Then moving to asparagines - ASN24, ASN36, ASN50, and ASN107 - examining their carbonyl and amide nitrogen positions relative to neighboring residues, and spotting a potential hydrogen bond between ASN107's OD1 and HIS105's NE2 based on the close distance.

Now checking GLN74's side chain geometry, finding a plausible hydrogen bond between its carbonyl and HIS65's ND1, then noting most serines and threonines are too small to worry about. I'm shifting focus to looking for steric clashes among the hydrophobic core residues, starting to catalog the terminal carbon positions of the valines, leucines, and isoleucines to compare distances between them.

I'm checking a few candidate distances near ILE102, VAL123, LEU94, and ILE104, but none are close enough to flag as clashes. Since nothing dramatic stands out yet, I'm switching strategy to scan for close CA-CA pairs by grouping residues into spatial regions and comparing within each cluster.

I find that ALA21's CA and GLY99's CA are only about 3.86 Å apart, which is unusually tight for CA-CA distance and worth investigating further at the atomic level. I'm now pulling the exact coordinates for ALA21 (N, CA, C, O, CB) and GLY99 (N, CA, C, O) to compute precise pairwise distances between their atoms, starting with CA-CA confirming ~3.86 Å and O-CA around 5.1 Å.

I'm computing several more atom-pair distances for residues 21 and 99, finding values ranging roughly from 3.99 to 5.0 Å, and confirming the minimum contact is the CA-CA distance of about 3.86 Å — tight, but since it exceeds the combined CA van der Waals radii (~3.4 Å), it's not a severe clash. I'm continuing to scan other CA pairs across the structure (residues 22-32, 24, 28, 93, 99, 101, 129, 131) checking for any distances close enough to suggest a clash.

Most pairs come back with distances safely above 4 Å, with one closer result of about 4.36 Å between residues 118/119 and 106, still within acceptable range. I'm continuing this systematic scan through more residue pairs (116, 117, 144, 148) to rule out any remaining close contacts.

I'm continuing to check pairwise distances between remaining coordinate points, computing differences to find close matches and ruling out the ones too far apart.

Nothing severe stands out from backbone comparisons, so the clash probably comes from side chains instead. I should build proper neighbor lists per residue based on CA-CA proximity under 10 Å, then systematically compare side-chain atoms against nearby residues rather than continuing ad-hoc pairwise checks.

Maybe the actual clash is subtler than expected, just a couple angstroms too close, so I check aromatic ring stacking distances that might be problematic. I'm measuring distances from PHE86's ring atoms to nearby residues like LEU116, ASN107, ALA109, and TYR78, but everything comes back within reasonable range. I then move to checking PHE75's ring against nearby residues like TRP53 and ILE71.

Continuing that pattern, I check more ring-to-ring distances between PHE47, PHE75, LEU43, TRP53, and ILE122/ILE71, but they all seem fine too. I then shift strategy to look for tight polar contacts like O...O or N...O pairs instead of ring clashes, reviewing salt-bridge and hydrogen-bond distances like LYS95-GLU22, HIS105-TYR32, and ASN107-HIS105, which all look normal. I'm now considering checking cysteine sulfur atoms in case there's an unusually close SG-SG distance between CYS120 and CYS121.

Since scanning residue pairs by hand is slow, I decide to try a more systematic grid-based approach: bucket all atoms into 4Å cubic cells based on their coordinates so I can quickly spot atoms from distant residues that end up unexpectedly close together.

I start binning the CA coordinates into 8Å cells across the residue range, computing cell indices for residues 19 through 28 to identify which ones cluster together spatially despite being far apart in sequence.

Continuing to convert each coordinate into its grid cell through index 82.

Continuing to convert each coordinate into its rounded grid cell, tracking how the path moves through integer space step by step.

I'm now wondering if the clash involves a specific residue like a proline or glycine, and considering whether this structure matches a known PDB entry with a documented clash score based on van der Waals radii overlap.

I'm checking specific distances: LYS95 NZ to GLU22 OE1 comes out to about 2.59 Å, likely a salt bridge rather than a true clash. I check a few more pairs like HIS105-TYR32 and ASN107-HIS105, finding distances around 2.8 Å, so I keep searching systematically for carbon-carbon pairs under 3.0 Å that would represent a real overlap.

Since side-chain tip comparisons haven't turned up anything below 3.4 Å, I try locating the protein's dense core by estimating the centroid of CA coordinates, then look at which residues cluster near that center—residues like 53, 122, 32, 71, 88, 105 seem to form the buried core, so I'm scanning their atoms for tight contacts and considering whether this fold resembles a beta-barrel or lipocalin-type structure.

Since exhaustive pairwise comparison hasn't found the clash, I decide to widen the search to include i,i+3 through i,i+6 sequence separations for turns and helices, and to check whether a charged side chain (Arg/Lys/Glu/Gln) might be poking into a neighboring loop's backbone. I'm also considering sorting all ~1049 atoms by z-coordinate into 3 Å slabs so I can systematically check for close x,y overlaps between non-adjacent residues within each slab.

I check ARG115's side chain atoms against nearby residues THR108, ALA109, LEU116, and ASP117, computing distances between their coordinates to see if any pair falls within clash range.

I move on to ARG58, ARG68, and ARG106, systematically comparing each guanidinium group's CB through NH1/NH2 coordinates against nearby side chains like TYR142, ASP145, THR44, GLU49, and ILE132, but none of these distances come out short enough to flag as a clash.

I then work through the aromatic rings of PHE138, TYR32, PHE35, PHE72, PHE124, PHE126, PHE147, and TRP148, checking each ring atom against neighboring residues' CB/CG/CD positions, but every distance I compute lands in the normal 3.3-4.4 Å range for legitimate packing rather than an actual clash.

Having not found a violation through spatial proximity of aromatic and charged side chains, I decide to switch strategy: I'll systematically go cell by cell through my spatial partitioning, checking CA-CA distances between non-adjacent residues under 6.5 Å and then examining their full atom-by-atom contacts, starting with ASN19, GLU21, and GLU22 in one spatial cell and comparing ASN19's OD1 position against GLU22's backbone and side chain atoms.
